title: Trophic Memory: How Damage Sticks to Deer Antlers
workingTitle: How Damage Sticks to Deer Antlers
audience: Readers who want regenerative biology explained with named experiments, not vibes — hunters, biologists, and anyone tracking bioelectric pattern memory.
metaDescription: Damage a deer antler, shed the rack, and next year an ectopic branch returns at the same spot. How trophic memory forces morphogenesis beyond gene-regulatory models.
angle: Treat the Bubenik antler series as a rare multi-year dataset on non-local pattern memory: location of injury → scalp/growth-plate storage → imprint on next year's bone decisions. Use Levin's CT-scanned inheritance of the collection as the irreproducible archive.

dataSources.name: Levin — Trophic memory, deer, and a truly unique scientific object
dataSources.notes: Primary narrative source: Bubenik discovery, 13-box antler transfer (2005 era contact; George A. Bubenik, Guelph), Tufts vet-school CT scans, growth rate 1–1.5 cm/day.

dataSources.name: Bubenik & Pavlansky 1965 / Bubenik 1990 (trophic memory)
dataSources.notes: Cited in Levin morphogenetic-fields review: injury mapped to subsequent ectopic tines; memory lasts years then fades.

dataSources.name: Levin — The bioelectric code (BioSystems)
dataSources.notes: Frames scalp growth-plate spatial memory across months and distance; contrasts molecular-pathway arrow models with target-morphology set-points.

dataSources.name: Karns & Ditchkoff — Trauma-induced malformed antler development (WSB)
dataSources.notes: Field confirmation language: velvet injuries often 'remembered' in later sets; abnormality progressively forgotten.

distribution.linkedinHook: Injure a specific point on a deer antler. It heals. The whole rack falls off. Next year: an ectopic branch at the same address. The memory cannot live in the bone that left.
distribution.shortFact: Adult deer regenerate antler bone, vessels, nerves, and velvet at ~1–1.5 cm/day — and can store injury location across years of shed racks (trophic memory).
